passages.title: Email Correspondence: A Cancelled Concert Series

emails.subject: Subscription refund — series 4, order 20831
emails.body:
Dear Box Office,

I hold a four-concert subscription to the Riverport Chamber Series, order 20831, purchased in September for $184. Two of the four concerts have now been cancelled: the November date, and the January date cancelled at four days' notice.

Your website states that cancelled performances are refunded or exchanged at the ticket holder's choice. When I telephoned on 28 January I was offered credit towards next season only. The person I spoke to was polite but said refunds were "not something we do for subscribers", which does not match what your own terms say.

I would like a cash refund for the two cancelled concerts. By my calculation that is $92, though if the subscription price was discounted against single tickets the pro-rata figure may differ, and I am content with whichever is correct provided the basis is explained.

I would add that I have subscribed for six years and intend to continue. I am not asking out of dissatisfaction with the series. I am asking because being told that a published policy does not apply to me was an odd experience and I would like it corrected in the record, not only in my case.

Regards,
Terence Nkemelu

emails.subject: RE: Subscription refund — series 4, order 20831
emails.body:
Dear Mr Nkemelu,

You were given wrong information and I am sorry. Our published terms say what you say they say, and they apply to subscribers exactly as they apply to single-ticket buyers.

On the amount: your subscription was priced at a fifteen per cent discount against single tickets, so the refund is calculated pro rata on what you actually paid rather than on face value. Two of four concerts is $92.00 — in this instance the two figures coincide, because the discount applies evenly across the series. Where a series carries a premium on one concert the figures do differ, which is the reason we calculate rather than halve.

The refund has been issued to the card used in September and will appear within five business days.

On your wider point, which I think is the more important one: the colleague you spoke to was repeating guidance given at a briefing in December, and that guidance was wrong. It has been withdrawn and re-issued, and every member of the box office team has been told directly rather than by email so that there is no doubt. Three other subscribers were told the same thing in January; we are contacting them today without waiting for them to ask.

Thank you for six years, and for raising this in a way that let us find the rest of it.

Regards,
Anneke Visser
Box Office Manager

passages.title: What Public Libraries Became
passages.content:
A visitor who had not entered a public library since the 1990s would find the building recognisable and its function substantially changed. Lending remains, but it is no longer what most of the floor space, or most of the staff time, is devoted to.

The shift began with a problem libraries did not choose. As other public services closed counters and moved online, the library was frequently the only municipal building left with open doors, no appointment system and nobody asking why you had come. People arrived needing help with benefit applications, immigration forms, job portals and tax filings, because there was nowhere else to go. Library staff absorbed that work without additional funding and often without training.

The result is a service whose stated purpose and actual function have drifted apart. Circulation statistics remain the metric by which many library systems are funded and judged, and circulation has been broadly flat or declining. Meanwhile visits, programme attendance and computer bookings have risen in many systems. A library judged on lending alone can look like a service in decline while being busier than it has ever been.

The demographic picture is not the one usually assumed either. Heavy library use is concentrated among two groups at opposite ends: parents of young children, who use it for programmes and for a warm indoor space that costs nothing, and adults over sixty-five. The lightest users are people between twenty-five and forty, who are also the group most likely to say in surveys that libraries are important and should be funded.

Nor is the digital question settled the way early predictions suggested. E-lending grew rapidly and then plateaued in most systems at well below half of circulation, partly because publishers charge libraries substantially more for digital licences than for physical copies, and those licences expire after a fixed number of loans. A physical book bought once may circulate for twenty years; a digital licence for the same title may cost three times as much and expire after twenty-six loans.

What the evidence supports is neither the elegy nor the triumphalism. Libraries are being used heavily, for purposes their funding formulas do not measure, by populations their advocates do not always describe accurately.

passages.title: Should a Fixed Share of Construction Budgets Fund Public Art?

viewpoints.name: Councillor Miriam Vasquez
viewpoints.text: We have had a one per cent for art requirement for eleven years and I would defend it, with one caveat. The strength of a fixed percentage is that it removes the annual argument — art is not competing against a bridge repair in every budget cycle, which is an argument it loses every time. The caveat is that the percentage produces the most money on the largest projects, which are usually roads and treatment plants in places nobody walks. We now pool a portion so it can be spent where people actually are.

viewpoints.name: Duncan Reilly, civil engineer
viewpoints.text: My objection is narrower than people expect. I am not against public art. I am against the money coming out of the construction budget while the maintenance liability comes out of the operating budget, permanently, with no provision made. Every sculpture is a cleaning contract, a repair schedule and eventually a removal cost. Fund the art, but fund its upkeep in the same decision, or you are handing a bill to whoever holds this job in twenty years.

viewpoints.name: Naomi Ferrante, artist
viewpoints.text: The percentage has been good for artists and I will not pretend otherwise. What it has also produced is a procurement process shaped for large firms — bonding requirements, insurance thresholds, portfolio criteria — that an individual artist cannot meet without a partner. So the money flows to a small number of studios that are effectively contractors. If the aim is a civic art culture rather than civic decoration, the process needs a route for people who have never delivered a million-dollar commission.

viewpoints.name: Errol Baptiste, community association
viewpoints.text: In my neighbourhood we got a piece nobody asked for, sited where the engineer said it would fit, and it was vandalised within a month. Two streets over, a mural developed with the school has been untouched for six years. The difference was not the budget or the artist; it was who was consulted and when. I am not opposed to the percentage. I am saying that spending it without asking the neighbourhood produces objects that the neighbourhood treats as somebody else's property, because that is what they are.
